content:
This is a sort of a Proof of Concept of a Zine-style for UTEP. It takes one concept, "Agency", and tries to incorporate that into different ideas/essays. Agency is a very dear concept to my heart, and that concept cannot be simply explored with one lens. As such, I've written 3 different essays on Agency that explore different aspects that I've learned about. The first focuses on Linux and Religion, The second focuses on Programming and Writing, and the third focuses on Concordat and Community. These are deliberately diverse, as the goal above all else is to explore: how does our different disciplines and realities clash and inform one another?

In the future, I'd like to have some artworks, poems, stories and the like that can explore future concepts as well. We are never bound to one medium for expression, and I'd like to feature as many of them as I can. Well, I'll see public interest first before I go any further.

For now, I sincerely hope you enjoy the zeroth publication of the zine, "Explication".

- Halley

*TABLE OF CONTENTS*
1. Linux: A Religious Perspective - Halley

https://forum.theeastpacific.com/t/writing-as-a-programmer/17927/1
3. Concordat: Crystallization of Community - Halley
https://forum.theeastpacific.com/t/concordat-crystallization-of-community/17928/1

content: The government should directly fund postsecondary education. Private colleges are fine but a robust public option is essential to well-educated and trained citizens. CRT is at this time a rather essential component of studies in its applicable fields, but isn't of much use in other fields. Higher education should include it in the relevant curriculum, but I don't think it would serve well as a general education requirement. "Half of all students from minorities" is an arbitrary standard that doesn't even come close to properly addressing faults in the distribution of education to citizens. The student body should be a representative sample of the population it is equipped to serve.

content:
Maturita Exam
Maturita is the name of the universal leaving qualification of four-year secondary schools and is a requirement for university studies and higher professional schools. It is made up of a number of subjects. Every student must take Czech language and world literature, consisting of a reading and grammar exam, a writing exam, and a literature oral exam. The second subject must be either mathematics or a foreign language (English, German, French, Spanish or Russian, including writing, reading, speaking and listening, to B1 level of the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages). The exams for these mandatory subjects are standardized and set by CERMAT. The other two or three exams taken by the student at this time are dictated by the school.

reminds me of this quote:

“Perhaps you have forgotten. That’s one of the great problems of our modern world, you know. Forgetting. The victim never forgets. Ask an Irishman what the English did to him in 1920 and he’ll tell you the day of the month and the time and the name of every man they killed. Ask an Iranian what the English did to him in 1953 and he’ll tell you. His child will tell you. His grandchild will tell you. And when he has one, his great-grandchild will tell you too. But ask an Englishman—” He flung up his hands in mock ignorance. “If he ever knew, he has forgotten. ‘Move on!’ you tell us. ‘Move on! Forget what we’ve done to you. Tomorrow’s another day!’ But it isn’t, Mr. Brue.” He still had Brue’s hand. “Tomorrow was created yesterday, you see. That is the point I was making to you. And by the day before yesterday, too. To ignore history is to ignore the wolf at the door.”
― John le Carré, A Most Wanted Man

content:
I would say it's really good, there are some places where I think you could utilize punctuation more, specifically maybe a question mark at line 4 to leave the reader hanging. The lack of commas combined with the syllabic imbalance make me read this very quickly, which works amazingly if that was your goal, but if it wasn't then I'd say add some pauses (commas, hyphens, or semicolons) and either break up your longer lines or merge your shorter ones.

Also, and this is completely personal preference, but I feel like it could've been much more concise and gotten the point across sooner without risking a loss of interest. The real question to ask is "was this poem meant to be read, or spoken?" And that should tell you what to focus on - if you want it to be spoken aloud, and you want it to be done a certain way, there should be more markers for the speaker so they can read it the way you intended. If the way it's read doesn't really matter to you, then I'd say it's pretty good right now as a skilled spoken word poet could take this and elevate it with the tools you've given them. If it's meant to be read, then I feel it could be trimmed a little to keep interest (people in general don't have great attention spans, especially not for poetry) and utilize a few more tools to guide the reader, especially punctuation and line breaks.

The last thing I'll say is poems are at their best when they break their own rules to deliver a message. There's a few points throughout where you go away from the rhyme scheme, which I think should be utilized more, utilized later on, and given more of a sense of direction.

Overall, though, good poem.

content: Thank you for clarifying - I'll attempt to address both points separately, even if we may still not see eye to eye here. Firstly: I think that's not an inherently invalid position, even if I personally am opposed to a greater number of GA resolutions, but I think it also takes away the necessity of those resolutions that means they are worthy of greater scrutiny - since they are not explicitly necessary and largely covered by previous legislation, one can hold them to a high standard when it comes to legislative practice, loopholes, etc. When a resolution is more fundamental to the WA, such flaws can more readily be excused for the greater good, but if the resolution is largely or even entirely redundant I think those should be strong considerations.

content: Nasicournia is a historical region whose story and accomplishments are portrayed in this Commendation through elegant prose, as is befitting of Westinor's style, one of the most prolific and experienced WA authors of our time. Though Nasicournia is no longer prominent in the NSGP sphere, its role in defending, especially within the Alliance Defense Network, cannot go unrecognized. Similarly amazing is Nasicournia's rich roleplay history, only some of which can be adequately captured within the proposal character limit. Nasicournia is well deserving of this Commendation and The East Pacific is convinced Westinor has written it to our exemplary standards and has done Nasicournia justice in this accounting. We stand with most of NS in voting FOR this proposal.

content: *Grea Kriopia's record in 10000 Islands and The Order of the Grey Wardens is not something to ignore. As a military leader and an internal leader, they have more than earned their time in the spotlight. Most importantly, their cultural contributions, such as the interregional Carnival of Celebrations, of which TEP is a consistent organizer, are truly remarkable. Much of their work goes unseen by the greater interregional community, but has a tremendous impact on the communities in which Grea Kriopia is a valued member. This resolution accurately and effectively presents the image of Grea Kriopia as a titan of gameplay. The East Pacific is emphatically FOR this proposal.*

content: *Dilber, quite plainly and simply, is a highly commendable nominee. Their work in TWP is admirable and comparable to that of some of the commended greats of TEP and other feeders. In various instances, particularly as Prime Minister, Minister of Foreign Affairs, and Delegate, Dilber has served the West Pacific and its people with strong foreign policy decisions, which are captured by author Giovanniland and co-author Overthinkers quite well in various clauses of the commendation. Their domestic accomplishments, such as engineering a TWP Delegate's lead in world endorsements, are equally noteworthy. Even so, the strongest part of the commendation describes Dilber's success in the august World Assembly, through tireless authorship and recognition that should not go unnoticed. The East Pacific acknowledges its past foreign affairs disagreements with the West Pacific, but cannot deny Dilber's accomplishments and the worthiness of this commendation. As such, we vote FOR.*

content: Im against this resolution. 1a doesnt make sense. A country could get around this by still banning almost all of these parts and say one single area or part of their environment is "nature" because it is a "natural feature".  They can ban being on beaches, in the woods, etc.  but have an allowance to hangout at a big natural rock and that's it and still be compliant. I dont think there should be unrestricted camping forced on nations either like in part 4. there are many reasons why you would want to prohibit camping in certain areas despite them being considered "nature" as defined in this law.

author: jowhatup

content: ```Refusing to draft a proposal on the forums goes against all World Assembly etiquette and sets a dangerous precedent for individuals with influence in the WA pushing through resolutions without scrutiny or diverse perspectives. Quorum raiding and queue stuffing were cited as concerns but quorum raiding is not prevented by failing to draft on the forums, as it takes place after submission anyway. Meanwhile, queue stuffing is not a legitimate concern since this is not a time-sensitive resolution either, like a Liberation or Injunction, where this argument would make sense. Some of the criticisms the proposal raises, such as the mention of a one-nation operation in Osiris, make sense, but others do not, as the authors would have heard had they respected the traditional process of drafting. Calling streak-breaking raids "largely inconsequential" is particularly tone deaf when one considers how those raids disrupt the stability of entire communities, and that those raids are mechanically identical to the 2022 attack on The North Pacific, which itself elicited interregional disapproval and condemnation. If a region's sovereignty is violated and the community suffers, foreigners have no right to call it "inconsequential" – it seems more like a Raider argument than a Defender one. Furthermore, The Black Hawks are far from mediocre – they are a significant part of NationStates history, which SC#217 captures. The East Pacific might not be so firm on that stance if the authors had allowed public comment and debate, which is the true arena by which resolutions are refined and strengthened. However, that did not happen, so we are forced to make judgments on elements that might have been changed if constructive dissent had been given an ear. The East Pacific will vote AGAINST this resolution.```

content:
Yodle is a name that many people outside of TRTHNBB and its diplomatic partners will likely not be familiar with. However, over the development of this proposal, Yodle’s exemplary deeds are given the worldwide spotlight they truly deserve. This proposal is a brilliant example of uplifting a diamond in the rough and demonstrating the hard work that goes into founding and maintaining a UCR with the cultural strength and political excellence of TRTHNBB, which has arisen as one of TEP’s most active and closest partner regions in recent days.

The proposal itself is well-written from the perspective of a region-mate familiar with Yodle’s work. Their resilience is highlighted immediately and developed over the course of the resolution. Their commitment to regionbuilding, including the Social Reformer, one of the most high quality regional newspapers in the game, a highly successful endotarting initiative, and their legislative legwork shines bright and true. It is not easy to create a successful region and there is no formula for it, but Yodle has risen to the challenge and met it.

Their flexibility and depth is showcased as well — not only is Yodle a titan on their own, but has been known to mentor and uplift the great leaders of their region as any good founder should, who form the core of the political population to this date and are all crucial as well to TRTHNBB’s recent diplomatic revolution. On top of it all, as a card collector, Yodle has distinguished themselves in yet another way worthy of praise, with many unique collections to their name.

The author has shown a great propensity to incorporate feedback and was keen from the start to hear from The East Pacific. For their hard work and that of Yodle, and for the great relationship we have developed with a region that would not exist, and certainly not in its current form, without the strong guidance of a figure such as them, The East Pacific is happy to vote FOR this resolution.

content:
The last time a TBH Condemnation was repealed, we submitted a scathing IFV criticizing the way its authors had spit in the face of this august body by flaunting tradition and sidestepping any legitimate criticism that could have arrived based on easily refuted excuses. Now, we stand here again facing a proposal that does the same. Equally, The East Pacific opposes this. We do not vote against this repeal because the resolution it targets is of high quality — indeed its quality is rather poor. We vote against because the repeal is no better. We could get into the flimsy substantial arguments and we could concede the strong points it makes between them, but the authors do not want that. If they did, they would have drafted this repeal on the forums.

The Black Hawks is deserving of a condemnation. Of that there can be no question. For years and years it has stood as one of the premier titans of raiding and its double condemnation status was a testament to that. Some argued that it maybe only deserved one. Some argued that one or both were of poor quality. But not until the recent trend of stripping raiders of recognition began did anyone suggest TBH was not worthy of one. In an ideal world, this repeal would be followed by a well-written replacement, which the authors are more than capable of. In that world, TEP might support a repeal and replace.

This is not that world. This is a world where petty R/D grievances rule all aspects of the game, where some military GPers wish to strip their opponents of their badges instead of acknowledging that they are effective foes. TEP will not parrot the raider talking points that this is meant to “make up for” poor performance on the field but we are firmly of the belief that it had no bearing on said performance. With or without this condemnation, the military landscape of this game will not change.

author: that_pers0n

content:
Though The East Pacific recognizes the storied history of Philosophers and its predecessor region, we do not see it as commendable based on the case made in this resolution.

Most of it discusses active debate and discussion, which is a good, supplemental point in its favor, but this appears to be the MAIN point in its favor within the proposal. Much of the resolution seems to be solely discussing the actions of the founder, as some in the forums have pointed out during drafting, and has little to do with the mutual construction of a commendable community — which is a high standard for regional commendations that must be met in our opinion.

Though this commendation is well-written, the region itself is not exceptional — if it is, the resolution has left out a lot of crucial information. For these reasons, The East Pacific recommends a vote AGAINST Commend Philosophers.

content:
```The Cards Community in NationStates represents some of the most dedicated people in the game. Farming and collecting cards is a practice requiring many hours of hard work and administrative maintenance. Vylixan/Sitethief is one of these dedicated members, whose collections represent diverse themes from card farmers and Pacifican Senators to SciFi and fantasy. The thousands and thousands of cards they own are physical proof of their exceptional accomplishments in the realm of Cards.

However, their collections aren't their only impressive accomplishments. Sitethief doesn't just hoard cards, but they give back to the community. Giveaways and pull events are some of the ways this can be done, which the Commendation authors document well, but Sitethief did not stop with that. Their technological contributions, between the projects they completed alone and the collaborative efforts they played important roles in, are representative of the innovation and dedication that the World Assembly should support.

The East Pacific believes Sitethief has more than exceeded our standards for commendability, and we are happy to support a unique resolution honoring a unique figure from our ally The New Pacific Order. For all of these reasons, TEP recommends a vote FOR this resolution.```

content: Thanks! As to interference with existing WA legislation, that's not just a personal standard of yours but a hard requirement for all proposals. The WA doesn't do amendments, instead a resolution must be repealed if changes are to be made to its policy. If you find that you can't do what you want to do without repealing #657, a repeal-and-replace is always taken more seriously when that replacement is already being developed.

content:
I need to be honest, I'm not sure how I feel about this one. It's certainly well thought and well written. My first impulse was that "countries should be able to ban this" and this resolution disallows that. But I don't want to be "ahhhh new technology bad, burn the witch." 

I wish I had been paying attention to the WA when this was being drafted because I actually have questions for once, but alas, that's my own fault, I suppose. What does "the WA Commission on Human Rights shall ensure member state laws are sufficient" mean? What power does that actually grant the Commission? 

I... am skeptical. I'm voting ❌ for now, but I could be convinced.

The Website is a list of the world's and everyone's problems, that get prioritized to the top of its lists by (basically being voted on) with a star rating system. Imagine if everyone had access directly to our leaders instantly every day. Those in charge would know exactly what's important to everyone without any doubt whatsoever. We would have a voice that we could point to and say "look, this many people, everyday use this medium and voice their opinion, it's equal, it's fair, it's just, and everyone who wants one gets a voice". Then our leaders would be able to and dedicate resources to the problems which make it to the top of the lists, and have the best solutions to all the problems already agreed upon, and things would just get done without any red tape, politics, shady backroom deals, or corruption. We would know what the most important issues are, in realtime, and we would know the best solutions for those problems, in realtime.The proprietary features are it's well traversable categories, search tree, & once a day you are able to vote from 1 to 100 stars on submittable lists of what you think the world, and others most important to solve problems are, only once per day. However you are also able to submit as many problems to the bottom of the lists as you want, and whichever problems have the most stars from the most people, get put at the top of the lists. Also you are able to submit as many solutions to each of the problems as you can think of, and the top solutions to the top world & other problems, with the most stars from the most people are put at the top of the solution list for each of the worlds, and others problems. Also the problems are traversable similar to an eBay search tree, and there are individually categorized & subcategorized priority lists made from the same proprietary star rating system, so that the website is incorruptible, and the data is irrefutable. I don't know about you, but if I have a problem, I would rather have my entire neighborhood, or rather the entire world helping me solve my problems, than me trying to come up with solutions to all my problems on my own, So that would be why anyone would be allowed to add what they think the best solution, to the solutions list that each problem will have, and everyone gets to rate the solutions on the list with the star rating system. Every minute of every day with the star rating system we will get to change our opinions once a day for each star rating, and have real time prioritized problems of the world and others. Also real time, the most agreed upon solutions, and real time and dedication of resources the most efficient way possible. This, will be, one day inevitably in the information age. There is no, more efficient way. There are also sub-categories besides just the major world issues for example groups that are individualized by categories that are searchable, and traversable similar to the way the eBay search tree is traversable and searchable, and the solutions that other people have submitted for those problems uses the proprietary star rating system making it all function more efficiently than we'll ever be able accomplish the world and others problems in any other way. The only thing more important than a system of this efficiency being in place, and functioning as the way we do things for the human race is clean free energy.

content:
🌐 = By 2134, humanity had checked off every checkbox on its wishlist: eternal life, faster-than-light travel, self-aware robots, and the ability to upload your consciousness like it was just another Spotify playlist.

But Max didn’t care about any of that as his bruised, bloodied self crash-landed on Orbital Station C-7 on Europa—a station known for being the hangout spot of drunkards. The kind of place space travelers end up when they want to forget whatever nearly killed them. And for Max, that involved shape-shifting aliens with bad attitudes and worse aims. But that was a story for another time.

Max stumbled into the bar where the lighting was as dim as the dusk on Earth, synth-jazz humming in the background, and gravity barely stable enough to keep his boots on the floor. He zombie-walked his way to the counter, slumping into a stool and exhaling like he'd been holding that sigh for a long time.

Then she appeared.

A female alien waitress, her skin a glowing pale blue, patterned with iridescent scales. Her eyes were wide, luminous yellow, and her long, flowing tendrils of hair shifted as if caught in a breeze.

Max froze in fear.

His brain hiccupped, his stomach twisted into a knot, and for a moment, all he could think of was the shape-shifting alien that had mimicked his ex and nearly killed him. The very same type of creature, standing before him. The urge to bolt hit him like a freight train, but he resisted.

Alien Waitress: "What would you like to order?"

Max’s voice came out a little too shaky. He tried to swallow the rising panic.

Max (grimacing in thought): "What the hell is it with aliens and bad timing?"

His mind raced.
Max in thought: “Stay calm, Max. It’s just a waitress. Just an alien waitress who’s probably very nice and not here to kill you”.
He shook his head in denial yet He could already feel the sweat dripping on his face, which the waiter was aware of.
Max (gritting his teeth, forcing a grin): "Your finest drink... preferably free."

The alien waitress tilted her head, her glowing eyes scanning him like a hawk eyeing down on its prey which startled Ma for bit as he takes note that She seemed to sense the shift in his body language but said nothing.

Alien Waitress: “Please make a selection from the menu.”

Max (still uneasy): “Okay, okay—whiskey. You know the real stuff?”

She glided away, and Max planted his elbows on the bar, rubbing his temples. He was halfway into his brooding when the doors behind him hissed open.

Metal boots clanked onto the metal floor while Max didn’t even attempt to put effort into looking behind him.

But then the clanking stopped right beside him as a male-presenting robot decked out in full cowboy attire—hat, duster coat, even a badge that said "Deputy Processor." Max finally glanced over to his right his eyes narrowing at the odd sight.

Cowboy Robot: “Evening, partner.”

Max: “You’re three centuries late for the Wild West convention.”

Cowboy Robot: “ What brings you here, pather?”

The alien waitress acknowledges the existence of the cowboy robot before going back to her business.

Max: * sigh* “I came here to drown my trauma with alcohol, not swapping lines with the cast of Westworld.”

The alien waitress returned, placing the glass of whiskey in front of Max—and another one or the cowboy robot as he thanked her with his Hollywood cowboy accent.

Max (glancing at the robot’s glass and then at the robot): “Wait—you can drink?!”

Cowboy Robot: “Sure can, pather! Though, I only drink for fun, pather .”

Max: “Perfect. A Hollywood Cowboy actor of a robot can drink. What’s next, you recite Shakespeare?”

The cowboy boot noticed the newspaper on the counter and picked up the newspaper to process it through his scanner from his blue robotic eyes.

Cowboy Robot: “ Say pather, Have you heard of Resolution #778?”

content:
🌐 = Max (slumping onto his stool, eyes narrowing as he looks around the bar): "Feels like I've been living in this godforsaken future for a century, and somehow, it's still all the same crap with passing Laws that don’t mean a damn thing!"

Cowboy Robot (adjusting his duster and looking genuinely excited): “Pather, let me tell you about the ‘Virtual Mind Convention, This is the future, pather!”

Max (eyes rolling, voice dripping with sarcasm): “Yeah, sure. A future where we’re all brain-dead in a server, debating who gets the right to charge us rent for our minds. ”
Cowboy Robot (leaning back, voice gravelly and serious): “Let’s start with the first part. The resolution defines ‘Virtual Mind’ as an uploaded, complete version of a sapient individual’s mind and consciousness into a computer or other electronic device capable of emulating the original mind of the individual. This ensures that any mind, regardless of the form it takes, retains its identity and rights.”

Max (eyeing him with a sceptical grin, swishing his whiskey): “Alright, I get it. But what the fuck is a 'sapient individual'? I mean, My ex used to call me one of those when I asked her what was for dinner. Was she just messin’ with me? And hold up—this ‘virtual mind’ thing sounds vague. If upload my dead goldfish’s mind, Does he get rights too? That little guy had dreams, you know.”

Cowboy Robot (gently adjusting his hat, unbothered): “The resolution’s about folks who can reason and reflect—sapient beings. Goldfish don’t quite cut, pather.”

Max (snorting, smirking): “Hey!, He has dreams… a tiny one to be exact.”

Cowboy Robot (pauses, processing Max’s words with a slow nod): “Well, digital consciousness is a big deal. We’re tryin’ to protect the rights of those who upload their minds. But... I suppose it ain’t as clear-cut as I first thought.”

Cowboy Robot (flipping to the next section): “Section 2’s a good one. It says an individual must give explicit written consent before their mind gets uploaded. No one’s bein’ forced into this.”

Max (leaning in, sarcasm dripping): “Oh sure, I’m sure no one wants to wake up in a server farm without giving the ol’ thumbs-up first. But what if someone changes their mind halfway through? Or what if some family member decides to upload Aunt Linda while she’s in a coma ‘cause they think it’s a good idea? This thing has more loopholes than my last tax return.”

Cowboy Robot (pausing, his mechanical eyes narrowing slightly): “You’ve got a point there... There are provisions for power of attorney, but it’s a little... shaky. Not airtight.”

Max (grinning): “Shaky? More like a sandcastle in a hurricane. I’m tellin’ you, this proposal’s full of holes. And now we’re trusting lawyers to decide whether my brain becomes a digital ghost?”

Cowboy Robot (musing, flipping the page, his voice less certain now): “Section 3 requires that any limitations imposed on a virtual mind must be followed. Violating that is a crime. You know, keeping the system clean...”

Max (chuckling, shaking his head): “Yeah, good luck with that. What if some tech-head decides to hijack someone’s brain for ‘data mining’? And we’re just supposed to trust that governments are gonna catch that? Hell, I’ve seen less corruption at a carnival dunk tank.”

Cowboy Robot (frowning slightly, his tone wavering): “Yeah... I see the problem there. The enforcement’s shaky. It’s harder than I thought to make this work...”

Cowboy Robot (trying to regain composure, flipping ahead): “Section 4 says that a virtual mind retains all the rights they had before uploading—like voting and owning property. Ain’t no difference from the real world.”

Max (leaning in, voice dripping with curiosity): “Okay, but what if my digital self decides to start a revolution? Am I still responsible for that? Or is digital ‘me’ a rogue agent now?”

author: aurorayukihime

content:
🌐 = Cowboy Robot (pauses, thinking deeply for the first time, his voice less robotic, more hesitant): “Well, the resolution says you still have your rights... but there could be complications. What if your digital self does something bad? Could it be you if you're just a copy?”

Max (raising an eyebrow, toying with his glass): “Bingo. What happens when my digital self starts a riot and I’m still here, having whiskey and talking to a robot? Who takes the heat for that?”

Cowboy Robot (staring into his glass, almost as if seeing the flaws now): “That’s... a tough question. I guess it’s still up in the air. The proposal doesn’t address that. Could be a big mess.”

Max (eyes narrowing, leaning in with a mischievous grin): “Now we’re gettin’ somewhere. So, you’re startin’ to see the cracks in this shiny ‘progress,’ huh?”

Cowboy Robot (almost hesitating, but nodding slowly): “Yeah... I didn’t want to admit it, but it’s clear now. It ain’t as perfect as I thought. Too many things they didn’t think through.”

Max (smirking, raising his glass): “There we go. The proposal’s a mess. A poorly-written, half-baked, digital trainwreck of a mess. Glad we’re on the same page.”

Cowboy Robot (softly clinking his glass as the realization sinks in): “Yeah. It’s gonna need a whole lotta work. More thought, more clarity. It’s like they tried to build a house with no blueprint.”

Max (grinning, shaking his head): “Exactly. So, here’s to fixin’ it. To a future where robots and humans get it right. Maybe.”

Cowboy Robot (smiling faintly, raising his glass): “To better laws and better minds, human and machine alike.”

Max (with a knowing look): “Cheers, cowbot.”

Cowboy Robot (now almost human in his tone): “Cheers, pather.”

So thanks for reading this I guess and vote for our repeal when you have the chance.

See ya.

content:
It's my opinion that bee-keeping is not a topic that the World Assembly should address specifically, it's overall too narrow when the WA can address ecological concerns more broadly, and domestic bee-keeping in particular is less useful for pollination than preserving wild pollinator populations.

IIRC, the target was written when Colony Collapse Disorder was a major concern for the future of  honey bees, however nowadays there is no concern for the continued survival of humanity's favored bee species, and instead it looks like wild insects species are most at risk of being wiped out. A resolution addressing this latter concern would be preferable.
searchtext:

content:
On further review, I've gone from "ambivalent" to "strongly opposed." The repeal arguments are unconvincing and borderline dishonest.
> Observing that Articles 2 and 3 of GA#657 require member states to decriminalise the possession and personal use of all recreational drugs (with limited exceptions), even if the people who consume them thereby endanger their health and continued survival,
Is that so? Let's take a look:
> No member nation may prosecute, punish, or penalise any individual for their consumption of a psychoactive drug, so long as such consumption occurs in private and **does not pose a clear, specific, and imminent danger to the health or safety of other individuals.**
I think it just barely isn't a veracity violation (not all cases of "endanger their health" rise to "clear, specific, and imminent") but it could be an interesting challenge. Also, while I hate to invoke RL data, imposing harsh penalties for drug possession does not effectively stop people from using those drugs and American laws to that effect are some of the most provably racist we have.
> Noting that one of the target resolution's rationales for doing so is that policies of criminalisation have failed to "actually reduc[e] drug addiction and use," even though GA#643 "Reducing Addiction" already requires member states to provide education about and rehabilitation from drug addiction (and will continue to do so after the passage of this repeal), and
Criminalizing drugs is effective because rehab exists? Huh? What? You might as well say "I am Groot"

content:
Not really feeling this one. The primary argument seems to be that member nations would have to hand over any information the WHA inspectors request of them, but given that requesting irrelevant information would be outside the mandates of the WHA, I don't see how this would be a problem. The other arguments are similar nothingburgers. 

On top of that, the repeal makes the confusing choice to both argue that members might not hand over any information except what is strictly required of them, *and* that the target is too intrusive in its demands, leaving me wondering whether the authors believe that nations should be required to hand over more or less information to the WA.

content:
I have no opposition to the text but ideologically I am opposed to regulating things at this level. 

What this proposal does is require energy providers in nations to make publicly available documentation on the risks of the energy they provide as well as ways to contact authorities for more information and for member nations to educate their citizens on the different types of energy and their risks. It then enables the WA Disaster Bureau to enforce these mandates. 

I do not believe this is something requiring the intervention of the WA. Reasonable nations would already be doing these things, and the international harm of nations which choose not to do so is relatively low.

content:
This is a plausible reading, but it's not a rational one, as it would make noncompliance assured. 

I think any reasonable nation would have to define conducting a study or an "independent survey" in such a way as to allow compliance in some fashion, and for that reason, I find the repeal's argument weak, but not illegal.

author: cretoxyrhin

content: I wrote a repeal of this [years ago](https://forum.nationstates.net/viewtopic.php?f=9&t=523911), which Simone later modified into [his own draft](https://forum.nationstates.net/viewtopic.php?f=9&t=538836) with my permission. This effort by Vara and co is completely independent of that. While I think the choice to focus on "diplomatic impunity" rather than more genuinely bizarre/dangerous stuff like "you have to prioritize random foreign aides over your own national leaders in emergencies and also can't do investigations" weakens this repeal, it's also targeting a genuine piece of crap that has a lot wrong with it to choose from, and there's merit to having a distinct angle to your own later draft on the same topic even if that angle isn't as strong (regardless of whether the different angle was intentional or coincidental). Maybe I'm just glad to see the target finally gone, but I'm personally in favor of this

author: cretoxyrhin

content: 747 does everything that 17 does, and it's way better written: it handles how funds are spent, what happens if there isn't enough funding, how to ensure transparency, and even has a proactive funding mechanism that doesn't force authors to waste characters saying "my proposal uses the general fund" and getting their resolution repealed because of how it handles funding (see [495](https://www.nationstates.net/page=WA_past_resolution/id=495/council=1)). I've been wanting someone to do proactive funding *forever* and Ice finally did it!
searchtext: 747 does everything that 17 does, and it's way better written: it handles how funds are spent, what happens if there isn't enough funding, how to ensure transparency, and even has a proactive funding mechanism that doesn't force authors to waste characters saying "my proposal uses the general fund" and getting their resolution repealed because of how it handles funding (see [495](https://www.nationstates.net/page=WA_past_resolution/id=495/council=1)). I've been wanting someone to do proactive funding *forever* and Ice finally did it!
author: cretoxyrhin

content: So that leaves 17 as an obsolete resolution that... bans deficit spending *for the WA* (not just the general fund; what a weird pseudo-blocker), has a weird half-assed reporting requirement, and has that dishonest "mandatory donations" requirement that doesn't provide a superadded benefit beyond "there shall be money" (which you kinda have to assume anyway for the WA to make any sense) and IMO actively hobbles things by being clumsily written. It's like spelling out a clumsy requirement in a normal resolution instead of having a committee do it. The way you spell out your requirement should be beneficial

content:
IFV - FOR (this is a test. If someone has a better idea of where to put these, I'm all ears):
```This repeal's target, GA 703, is certainly verbose, technical, and micromanage-y to a significant degree even by GA standards (kinda predictable considering who wrote it). Its title, "Consular protection [sic] Arrangements," is misleading considering it covers a wide hodgepodge of accommodations members are required to extend to all foreign citizens within their borders, even if said citizens are from a non-member state. These accommodations range from the bizarrely narrow, such as occasionally setting up private meetings between citizens accused of crimes and diplomatic staff, to concerningly broad stuff like facilitating any adoptions permitted under international law and assisting with "repatriations in an emergency if a citizen lacks the means to do so," including shuttling corpses around.

The repeal itself relies on weaker arguments than we'd like. There are numerous boilerplate appeals to national sovereignty where arguments specifically tailored to the provisions in question would be more effective, or where those appeals are unnecessary supplements to otherwise decent arguments. The complaints about the target overreaching are compelling, but the lack of any mention of the nebulous nature of "offer assistance" is odd. We would've also liked to see mention of the obvious loophole in "[t]he assisting state deems itself capable of offering such assistance."

That said, the arguments the repeal does use are still sufficiently convincing. It helps that the target reads like something pumped full of enough helium to lift a small blimp.```

content:
> Concerned that GA#52 merely requires the International Food Welfare Organization to distribute "food rations to the people of nations undergoing severe economic depression, famine, or conflict which causes a shortage of food" without also requiring them to be culturally sensitive, nutritious, or even free from outside poisons,
Shamelessly exploiting the committee rule getting axed, don't you just love it? In what world does giving a WA body the authority to provide food mean that WA body is going to lace the food with poison? The organization isn't even required to distribute those surpluses in a particular way. The authors could've convincingly argued that establishing a vague surplus donation system with no elaboration is problematic. Instead, they went for this drivel.
> Angered that GA#52 declares that where "a compelling governmental interest exists to protect the health and welfare of the people, the right of governments to seize food to supply to victims of such crises is granted, so long as such seizure is not detrimental to the larger population," effectively allowing states to steal food from private entities - such as businesses, charities, and middle-class individuals - without regards to any nutritional or other assistance they may have received from abroad, and in particular while demanding the pre-existence of such a "compelling government interest" as will almost inevitably arise during such crises,
Stealing food from vulnerable people during a crisis would both fail to satisfy the compelling interest and be detrimental to the population. And if they've received sufficient nutritional and other assistance from abroad then there's no crisis anymore, is there? The "middle-class individuals" part is a nice touch 🙄

Imagine the consequences for sewage systems

> Confused, however, at the lack of criteria put in place for validating works uploaded to the ULC, allowing the acceptance of works with no factual or useful information, reducing the ease of locating beneficial works for actual use, and overwhelming the administrative and computational systems that back up the ULC with the amount of pointless archived text allowed,
This is true, but the entire point of the ULC is to be an internet archive (no expensive physical facilities). content:
```Some resolutions are flawed because of minor writing issues that have less than ideal consequences. GA 111 is flawed because it kneecaps research before tossing it in a lake.

This repeal competently goes through the many, many problems with the target, from the staggeringly massive such as requiring every single [i]prospective[/i] researcher in every single field to file documentation to an Institutional Review Board for medical research, to the still significant such as banning any research that involves "significant physical damage," to the more anodyne such as lacking an appeals process. Impressively, it manages to articulate all this without coming off as bloated or making any one argument sound less important than the rest.

We'd be tempted to support this repeal anyway due to its author being a TEPer, but its excellent quality makes that decision easy.```

> The vague definition of “very low intelligence” in Article 2.1 allows governing bodies within a nation to oppress minority groups by declaring them legally incompetent according to a supposed standard of intelligence, which is especially worrying as there is no objective standard for intelligence or what constitutes “very low intelligence”, making it easy to manipulate this definition for malicious purposes;
This is better than the old version, but a term not being defined doesn't mean governments can just make up whatever they want. You might as well repeal every resolution for not recursively defining every single word in it

content:
@WA Notification @deleted-role 

Hello all!

Some of you may not have known, but it is my intention to stay on as WAA Minister when Shadow's term ends - ever since I entered this position, it's been my dream to revitalise, reform, and renew it and encourage local WA participation in TEP. We're in a position now where we can take advantage of a sprawling global WA environment to further the international standing of TEP and the region's WA influence.

To strengthen WA involvement, I'd like to introduce a weekly WA discussion. These would usually occur every week, with a new question every Monday, and what we'd do is we would talk about a certain proposal / draft (or group of proposals or drafts) in the WA forums and, most importantly, TEP's eventual stance on it if it were to reach quorum. If we can get a head start on potential future resolutions, it'll put us in a good spot!

Please react with a :pandagrape: below if you'd be interested in such a weekly discussion, which would take place in #wa-voting, or if you'd be interested in helping the WA department organise it at all!
